content: The number of precancer treatments in the general population was assessed as part of the PICO 5 framework, specifically focusing on post-treatment follow-up. All women who tested positive and were treated after visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) to determine eligibility were included. Women who were triage-positive were referred for colposcopy. Those who were VIA triage-positive were treated based on VIA eligibility criteria. Women testing positive for HPV types 16/18 were treated following VIA-based eligibility determination. Women with other high-risk HPV (OHR) types were treated only if they were VIA triage-positive. It is important to note that some women required multiple treatments during follow-up. Screening strategies included 5-yearly HPV triage for women aged 30–50 years, with variations in intervals and age groups (e.g., 10-yearly screening for ages 30–50 or 35–45). Cost-effectiveness was evaluated using cost per health-adjusted life year (HALY) across all scenarios. Outcomes were measured over the lifetime of a cohort of 100,000 women, including cervical cancer cases, cervical cancer deaths, precancer treatments, additional preterm deliveries due to precancer treatment, and the number needed to treat (NNT) to avert a cervical cancer death. Discounted lifetime costs were also calculated. For cervical cancer cases and deaths, the percentage reduction was compared to no screening, while for precancer treatments, NNT, and costs, the percentage difference was compared to the baseline scenario (12-month follow-up with HPV testing). Strategies showed similar effectiveness (less than 5% difference) in reducing incidence and mortality across variations of test-of-cure management within the same primary test-triage group. However, using cytology and HPV co-testing for post-treatment follow-up increased the number of precancer treatments, NNT, and associated costs. The first set of numbers in each box represents the percentage change compared to no screening, while the second line represents the difference compared to baseline scenarios. For cervical cancer cases and deaths, the percentage in brackets in the second line indicates the difference in percentage change versus no screening. For precancer treatment, NNT, and cost columns, it indicates the percentage difference versus the baseline for that flowchart. In summary, general population screening strategies, such as 10-yearly screening for ages 30–50 or 35–45, were evaluated. The outcomes included cervical cancer cases, deaths, precancer treatments, NNT, and discounted lifetime costs. The effectiveness of strategies was consistent across variations, with cytology and HPV co-testing increasing precancer treatments, NNT, and costs.
